overview: This single-page file inventory lists papers concerning Japanese newspaper clippings and press commentary in 1938–1939. The indexed documents include translations from Nagoya’s vernacular press on Japanese military operations in China and on local military industry and labor, as well as reports of Japanese press reactions to American policy toward Japan’s activities in China, possible U.S. alignment with Britain and France against the totalitarian states, American financial measures in South America, and the proposed extension of the Export-Import Bank’s charter.

people.name: Stephan

subfiles.title: List of papers on Japanese newspaper clippings
subfiles.about: An inventory identifies four reports or cross-references concerning Japanese press coverage of military, labor, diplomatic, and financial-policy questions in 1938–1939.
subfiles.summary: The first two entries record December 1938 reports from Stephan at Nagoya containing translations from the local vernacular press on Japan’s operations in China and on Nagoya’s military industries and labor. A February 1939 telegram from Grew reports Japanese press commentary on American attitudes toward Japanese activities in China, possible cooperation among the United States, Great Britain, and France, and alleged U.S. plans to restrict Japanese, German, and Italian influence in South America. A final entry cross-references related material on extending the charter of the Export-Import Bank of Washington and a letter from the Secretary to the chairman of the Reconstruction Finance Corporation.

interest: The page is useful as a provenance and reconstruction aid because it records the dates, origins, and subjects of documents that are not themselves present in the supplied OCR. Its juxtaposition of local Nagoya reporting with embassy-level analysis shows how the State Department collected both regional economic information and national press reactions. It also reveals the close connection officials drew between the war in China, emerging anti-totalitarian alignments, and American financial influence in Latin America on the eve of the Second World War.
